memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: And when the Israelites heard that they had built the altar on the border of Canaan at Geliloth near the Jordan on the Israelite side, the whole assembly of Israel gathered at Shiloh to go to war against them. — Josh 22:11-12 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Word reaches the western tribes: the eastern tribes have built an altar. Immediately, the whole assembly gathers for war. Not a letter. Not a question. Straight to the sword. They assumed the worst — that their brothers had fallen into idolatry and rebellion — and they were ready to fight over it.

We should be honest about how quickly this escalated. These were brothers who had fought side by side just days before. Yet a single report, without a conversation, nearly plunged them into civil war. How easily unity can shatter when we assume the worst about one another.

How often we do the same. We hear a report, we imagine the worst motive, and our hearts move to conflict before we have asked a single question. Relationships in families, churches and friendships are wounded again and again by conclusions we reached too fast.

Yet, as we will see, God's grace is at work even here — because before drawing the sword, they will send messengers to ask. Scripture calls us to be quick to listen and slow to become angry (Jas 1:19). Love does not rush to think evil of others (1 Cor 13:5-7). Before you assume the worst about a brother or sister, ask. The truth may be very different from your fear.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you tend to assume the worst when you hear a troubling report?
2. When did asking a question save you from a wrong conclusion?
3. How can you be quicker to listen and slower to judge?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, forgive me for how quickly I assume the worst about others. Make me quick to listen, slow to anger, and eager to seek the truth in love. Amen.
